level-1.title: Choosing to save or to spend
summary: Every rupee you spend is a rupee you cannot save.
A savings goal is a thing you are saving for, with a price and a date.
Write the goal down. A bicycle costs ₹4000. You save ₹200 each month.
₹4000 divided by ₹200 is 20. So the goal takes 20 months.
Small spends add up. ₹20 a day is ₹600 in one month.

questions.prompt: A bicycle costs ₹4000. You already have ₹800 saved, and you save ₹200 more each month. How many more months until you can buy it?

image.alt: A bicycle with a price tag and some coins already saved

options.label: 16 months
8 months
20 months

questions.hint: First subtract what you already have, then divide by the monthly saving.

questions.prompt: You spend ₹20 a day on snacks and ₹15 a day on games, every day for 30 days. How much MORE do you spend on snacks than on games that month?

image.alt: A snack and a game token side by side

questions.hint: Find the daily difference first, then multiply by 30 days.

questions.scenario: Meena has ₹600 for a school bag needed in two months. The bag costs ₹1,000. She can save ₹200 each month. A game she wants costs ₹300.
questions.prompt: Which plan gets Meena the bag on time?

options.label: Keep the ₹600 and save ₹200 each month
options.consequence: After two months, Meena has ₹1,000 for the bag. She can plan for the game afterwards.

options.label: Buy the game and keep saving ₹200 a month
options.consequence: After buying the game, ₹300 remains. Two more deposits bring the total to ₹700, leaving a ₹300 gap.

options.label: Buy the game and save ₹100 a month
options.consequence: Meena ends with ₹500. Reducing the monthly saving makes the gap larger.

questions.hint: Start with what remains after the purchase. Then add two months of saving.

reasoning.prompt: Why does keeping the ₹600 work for this goal?

options.label: Buying a game is always a bad use of money.
The money already saved plus two deposits covers the price by the deadline.
The bag will probably cost less in two months.

reasoning.hint: Use the stated price and date, without assuming a discount.
reasoning.explanation: ₹600 + ₹200 + ₹200 = ₹1,000. The issue is the deadline and the available money, not whether games are good or bad.

level-2.title: Saving, spending and opportunity cost
summary: Opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose.
If you spend ₹500 on headphones, the opportunity cost is the game you did not buy.
Pay yourself first means you save before you spend.
A common plan is to save 20 rupees out of every 100 you receive.
An emergency fund is money kept only for surprise problems.

questions.prompt: You earn ₹1000 and follow pay-yourself-first at a 20% rate, saving first and then spending ₹500 on headphones from what is left. What is the true opportunity cost of the headphones?

image.alt: Headphones next to a game box, with a savings jar already filled

options.label: The full ₹1000 you earned
The other thing worth ₹500 you could have bought with your spending money
The ₹200 you saved

questions.hint: Opportunity cost only concerns the money you chose to spend, not the money you saved first.

questions.prompt: You earn ₹1000 and follow pay-yourself-first at a 20% savings rate. How much do you save BEFORE spending anything?

image.alt: Money going into a savings jar before any spending happens

questions.hint: 20 percent of 1000 is saved first, before any spending happens.

questions.scenario: Arjun has ₹800 in emergency savings and ₹400 saved for a game. His phone breaks and he needs it repaired before tomorrow’s schoolwork. Repair costs ₹800. The game is on sale for ₹400 today.
questions.prompt: How should Arjun handle these two costs?

options.label: Buy the game first and leave the repair until later
options.consequence: The sale ends today, but buying the game leaves the school communication problem unresolved.

options.label: Use ₹400 of emergency savings for the game and postpone the repair
options.consequence: Only ₹800 remains across both pots. Using emergency money for the game also delays a needed repair.

options.label: Pay for the repair from the emergency pot, then plan to refill it
options.consequence: The phone works again. The ₹400 game savings remain, but the emergency pot now needs rebuilding.

questions.hint: Which cost is an unexpected problem that affects school? Which cost can wait?

reasoning.prompt: Why use the emergency pot for the repair?

options.label: It is an unexpected necessary cost; the sale does not make the game an emergency.
Anything priced at ₹800 counts as an emergency.
Using emergency savings means there is no need to save again.

reasoning.hint: Look at what the money is for, rather than just the price.
reasoning.explanation: The repair restores access to school messages. After using the buffer, Arjun should plan how to rebuild it. What he does with his game savings is a separate choice.

level-3.title: Saving with a goal and a date
summary: Saving works best with a goal, an amount and a date. "Save more" is a wish. "₹3,000 by Diwali" is a plan.
Divide the goal by the months you have. ₹3,000 in 6 months is ₹500 a month.
A big cost that comes once a year, like school fees or a festival, can be saved for a little every month. This is called a sinking fund.
An emergency fund should cover about three to six months of basic costs, not just one surprise.
Lifestyle creep is when spending rises every time income rises, so saving never grows. When you get more, raise your saving first.
Waiting for a reward is hard. A plan with a date makes it easier, because you can see the finish line.

questions.prompt: You want a ₹4,800 bicycle in 8 months. How much must you save each month?

image.alt: A bicycle with a price tag beside a calendar

questions.hint: Divide the total price by the number of months.

questions.prompt: School fees of ₹6,000 are due every June. What is the smartest way to be ready?

image.alt: A calendar with June circled and a fee bill

options.label: Borrow the full amount from a friend in June
Hope for a gift before June
Set aside ₹500 every month, so it is ready by June

questions.hint: Think about splitting one big cost into twelve small ones.

questions.scenario: A family has ₹1,000 left after this month’s essentials. A known school cost of ₹3,000 is due in six months. Its emergency pot was recently emptied. There are no savings yet for the school cost.
questions.prompt: Which plan starts both savings pots this month and meets the school goal with equal monthly deposits?

options.label: Save all ₹1,000 for emergencies and start school saving next month
options.consequence: The buffer grows faster now, but the school goal will need ₹600 a month over the five remaining months.

options.label: Set aside ₹500 for school and ₹500 for emergencies
options.consequence: The school goal gets one of six planned ₹500 deposits, and the emergency buffer starts growing too.

options.label: Spend ₹500 on extras and put ₹500 into emergencies
options.consequence: The buffer starts growing, but nothing is reserved for the known school bill this month.

questions.hint: Split the known bill across six months, then see what remains for surprises.

reasoning.prompt: Why keep the school savings separate from the emergency pot?

options.label: Saving for school can wait because the emergency pot will cover any bill.
An equal split will keep working even if the price or deadline changes.
A dated school bill is predictable; the emergency pot is for costs not already planned.

reasoning.hint: Compare a cost with a known date to a surprise cost.
reasoning.explanation: ₹3,000 over six months needs ₹500 a month. Separate purposes make it easier to see whether both goals are funded. The equal split fits this example, not every family.
